items.title: Mythical mountain god inspires name for China's first freshwater cave snail

items.title: What's in the dust? Study finds hidden metals in city streets
items.summary: If you're in an urban area with strong winds, chances are you are breathing in more than a little dust. You could be exposed to metals from cars, construction sites or pesticides used decades ago.

items.title: Seaweed-derived coating keeps strawberries fresher than a fridge
items.summary: University of British Columbia researchers have developed an edible, seaweed-derived coating that can keep strawberries fresh for at least four days at room temperature, outperforming uncoated berries stored in the refrigerator.

items.summary: Fungal diseases that affect grain crops can be devastating to global agriculture and food security. Fungicides are the most common preventive measure, but as fungal diseases become more prevalent, the pathogens become increasingly resilient.

items.summary: An international study led by Flinders University has found a fertile area of inspiration to explain an important step in evolution—and it's a whole lot of poop. items.title: Q&A: Gen Z puts high priority on jobs with meaning, purpose, but sees daunting hurdles
items.summary: Among Gen Z, 79% want a job mainly focused on helping people or making a positive difference in others' lives. But only about half of workers ages 18–29 who want such a position say they have one.

items.title: What makes us happy?
items.summary: Maybe to some degree. But a new international study suggests the communities we live in matter a whole lot, too. Researchers analyzed responses from 97,220 people across 66 countries and identified five broad factors associated with happier societies.

items.title: Repetitive genomic regions link structural genomic variation to species diversity
items.summary: Researchers sequenced the genomes of three medaka, or Japanese rice fish, a common model organism used in biological research, nearly 10 and 20 years ago. While sequencing the genomes was relatively straightforward, assembling them was anything but.

items.title: Cancer-fighting chewing gum cuts HPV levels by up to 93%
items.summary: A specially engineered chewing gum reduced HPV by up to 93% and nearly eliminated two bacteria linked to head and neck cancer. The treatment preserved beneficial mouth bacteria, raising hopes for a safer and more affordable therapy.

items.title: Iron and cobalt both curb stainless invar expansion, but iron leads
items.summary: Invar alloys resist expanding or contracting with temperature, a property valuable for precision instruments, but it has been unclear how this "invar effect" plays out separately in each element of complex, multimetal stainless invar alloys.

items.summary: A tiny 518-million-year-old sea creature has revealed the earliest known evidence of the structures that eventually became spiders’ fangs. items.title: This hydrogen turbine turns controlled explosions into electricity
items.summary: Scientists have successfully generated electricity with a hydrogen turbine that produces its own pressure through detonation waves instead of relying on a mechanical compressor. The breakthrough could unlock dramatically more efficient power systems for clean energy and future aviation.

items.title: Fire department leaders drive crew fitness, study finds
items.summary: For firefighters, physical fitness is a matter of safety, survival and long-term health. While past research has largely focused on individual habits, a new study has revealed that station leaders play a critical role in shaping firefighters' physical readiness.

items.title: Antibiotic-resistant seafood bacterium found in Vietnam fish farming waters near popular island destination

items.title: These underwater bones could solve a mystery about extinct giants
items.summary: Animal bones preserved in South Australia’s underwater caves reveal distinctive clues shaped by darkness, algae, bacteria, and other environmental conditions.
